days.label: Friday, October 23
days.note: New sites today: Damn Interesting, Lapham's Quarterly, JSTOR Daily, Sky Sports F1, Grande Premio, Formula One History, and a handful of small sites off the Hacker News front page, plus two F1 podcasts new to the list, Up To Speed and The Race F1 Rewind. Practice starts in Austin today, and the Horner memoir fallout continues.

hero.alt: An orange canoe on a calm fjord below steep mountains in Gudvangen, Norway
hero.caption: Still water, Norway

items.t: Could a Single Shade of Black Help the Outdoor Industry Unite?
items.d: Every outdoor brand dyes its own nearly identical black fleece, and Haglofs and Polartec want everyone to just share one. A smart look at the hidden plumbing behind your favorite jackets, and whether rival brands can ever agree on anything. About 1,300 words, 6 minutes.

items.t: The Most Badass New Performance Truck Doesn't Come from Ford, Chevy or Ram
items.d: Brabus stretched a G-Wagen by 20 inches, gave it a bed and a 900 hp twin-turbo V8, and will build exactly ten. Pure automotive excess, with the specs and interior details to back up the headline. About 650 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Into the Karakoram: One Designer's Unlikely Education at the Roof of the World
more.d: A Slovenian pack maker joins a mountaineer on a Gasherbrum expedition that falls apart at altitude, and the story of how she got there (a Patagonia repair shop, custom packs built from guide feedback) is the real payoff. About 2,700 words, 12 minutes.

more.t: OluKai's Moto-Ready, Master Bladesmith-Approved New Work Boot Boasts a Life-Extending Design
more.d: A $300 resoleable work boot designed with a Hawaiian bladesmith, sized up against the Danner Moto Wedge it clearly wants to beat. Good read if you like gear built to be rebuilt rather than replaced. About 550 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Audemars Piguet Is Taking a Page Out of Rolex's Book
more.d: Rolex's certified pre-owned program is pulling in roughly $229 million a quarter, and AP looks set to copy it. A quick explainer on why buying a used Royal Oak may soon get a lot less sketchy. About 400 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: Relwen Blends Two Vintage Military Jackets into a 2-in-1 Masterpiece
more.d: An M65 field jacket shell with a quilted bomber liner that works on its own, done in technical fabrics so the vintage look actually performs in fall weather. Fun jacket-nerd detail on how the two pieces fit together. About 600 words, 3 minutes.

items.t: See Inside Cells Like Never Before in These Vivid Microscopic Images
items.d: The winners of this year's Nikon Small World contest, including a time-lapse of mitochondria and chloroplasts streaming through plant leaf cells. Mostly pictures and video with light, friendly captions, about 1,200 words, 5 minutes.

items.t: Artemis II Results Show How Much Science People Can Do at the Moon
items.d: The first science from the crewed lunar flyby: the moon's colors, tiny impact flashes, a solar eclipse seen from space, and the surprising value of astronauts' sketches and spoken notes over cameras alone. About 1,600 words, 9 minutes.

more.t: MMX Mission to Reveal the Origins of the Martian Moons
more.d: A deeper follow-up to yesterday's Phobos story: Ethan Siegel walks through the two rival ideas for where Mars got its lumpy little moons (captured asteroids or a giant impact) and why the orbits point to a smash-up. About 3,000 words, 13 minutes, no math.

more.t: Watch Humpback Whales Team Up With Sea Lions to Hunt
more.d: In Monterey Bay, sea lions herd anchovies into tight balls and humpbacks lunge straight through them, and both sides seem to come out ahead. Quick read with video, about 300 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: How Crocodiles Survived the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs
more.d: Researchers matched 7,000 fossils against 245 million years of climate models to figure out why crocs made it through the extinction: they mostly moved toward warmer places. Fun dinner-table fact for the kids. About 430 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: A New Fossil Hints at the Surprising Origins of Snakes
more.d: A tiny 75 to 85 million year old snake ancestor from Brazil has a reinforced skull and weak eyes, which says it was a burrower, so early snakes had already split into different lifestyles. About 475 words, 3 minutes.

items.t: Lofty Ambitions: The Man Who Tried to Fly a Biplane to Everest and Climb It Alone
items.d: In 1933 Maurice Wilson, a WWI veteran who had barely learned to fly, pointed a secondhand biplane at Everest, convinced that faith and fasting would carry him to the summit solo. When officials impounded the plane he sold it and walked into Tibet instead, and what happened next is one of the strangest stories in mountaineering. About 4,000 words, 19 minutes. New site for this list.

more.t: South Polar Times: The Handmade Magazine That Kept Scott's Men Sane Through the Antarctic Winter
more.d: Anne Fadiman on the typed, hand-illustrated magazine that Shackleton edited and Edward Wilson drew for Scott's expeditions, full of parodies, verse, and in-jokes to beat the months of polar dark. A warm, funny look at how a crew builds morale from nothing. About 4,500 words, 20 minutes. New site for this list.

more.t: The Unceasing Cessna Hacienda: 64 Days in the Air Without Landing
more.d: In 1958 a Las Vegas hotel owner paid two pilots to keep a modified Cessna 172 aloft for as long as humanly possible, refueling from a speeding truck on a desert road and sleeping in shifts. They stayed up for 64 days and set a record nobody has broken. About 4,000 words, 19 minutes.

items.t: Little Rules About Big Things
items.d: Roughly 90 one-line Morgan Housel observations on wealth, debt, compounding, housing and investor psychology, each one a conversation starter. Evergreen and easy to dip in and out of. About 2,300 words, 10 minutes.

items.t: Playing the Wrong Game
items.d: Nick Maggiulli, newly a dad, uses competitive sauna and freediving deaths to ask why we chase status games whose rewards are visible and whose costs are hidden. A sharp behavioral finance read on what you are optimizing for in your 40s. About 1,000 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: 15 Year Stock Market Returns
more.d: Ben Carlson lines up the S&P 500's 3, 7, 10 and 15 year returns against the 50 year average and shows how far above trend this run has been. A quick, sober case for dialing down your return assumptions now, which costs nothing if he is wrong. About 500 words, 3 minutes.
more.m: A Wealth of Common Sense, Oct 18

more.t: Can the new Bill Bengen Portfolio Increase My Withdrawal Rate to 4.7%?
more.d: Big ERN stress tests Bengen's new 55/40/5 small-cap and international tilt and finds the higher safe withdrawal rate leans on small-cap alpha that may not persist. Deep retirement math for a weekend coffee, with his own failsafe numbers at the end. About 7,000 words, 30 minutes.

more.t: Your Financial RPE
more.d: A CFP who spent 20 years as a personal trainer borrows rate of perceived exertion to ask how hard you are really working on the money tasks that matter, like estate planning, versus the ones that feel productive. Short and a little uncomfortable in a good way. About 650 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Investing Lessons from 36 Years at Morningstar
more.d: Jim Dahle interviews retired Morningstar research VP John Rekenthaler on fees, why TIPS look attractive at today's real yields, his skepticism of private investments, and his own retirement setup. Full transcript on the page if you would rather read than listen. Runtime 84 minutes.

items.t: MPH: The fastest F1 car at COTA? Everyone is pointing somewhere else
items.d: Mark Hughes on the Friday-morning guessing game in Austin, where Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes each insist a rival has the quickest car and the bumpy COTA surface may decide who is right. Written today, about 850 words, 5 minutes.

items.t: Christian Horner reveals Red Bull talks with Lewis Hamilton's management before telling Niki Lauda to sign him for Mercedes
items.d: The juiciest bit of Horner's new memoir so far: Red Bull quietly sounded out Hamilton's camp, chose Vettel and Webber instead, and Horner then nudged Lauda toward the signing that built the Mercedes dynasty. About 900 words, 5 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: Marko fires back at Horner and calls explosive Red Bull memoir a collection of untruths
items.d: The other side of the Horner book: Helmut Marko's rebuttal plus a tidy history of how the two men's feud grew from Mateschitz's death to both of them being out of Red Bull by 2025. Pure paddock soap opera, about 1,200 words, 7 minutes. New site for this list.

more.t: How Antonelli levelled up his character to be F1 2026's world champion-elect
more.d: Filip Cleeren argues that Antonelli's five-win opening blitz is less impressive than the composed drives in Baku, Sepang and Singapore once the Mercedes advantage faded. Good context before a possible coronation this weekend, about 1,000 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: Drive: a review of Christian Horner's long-awaited F1 memoir
more.d: A proper book review rather than another extract: what the memoir covers (Marko, Jos Verstappen, the Alonso and Leclerc near-misses, the rejected Lauda offer) and whether it is worth your money. About 800 words, 4 minutes.

more.t: Christian Horner reveals George Russell Red Bull talks amid Max Verstappen rumours
more.d: One more memoir nugget: Horner rang Russell's representatives at Silverstone 2025 while Wolff was courting Verstappen, days before Horner was fired. A neat window into how the 2026 grid nearly looked different. About 750 words, 4 minutes.

more.t: Antonelli's second-year title bid reminds Hamilton of his first seasons in F1
more.d: Hamilton on his Mercedes successor possibly winning the title in year two, just as he did in 2008, and on the support system that made it possible. Quote-heavy but a nice bit of symmetry, about 500 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Who are F1's youngest world champions?
more.d: A ranked tour of the ten youngest champions, from Vettel's 2010 record (23 years, 134 days) through Hamilton, Alonso and Jim Clark. Handy history if Antonelli, at 20, rewrites the top of this list in Austin. About 3,000 words, 15 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: Up To Speed: Christian Horner Full Interview, Red Bull Exit, Verstappen and an F1 Return?
items.d: Horner's first podcast interview since leaving Red Bull, with David Coulthard and Naomi Schiff asking about Abu Dhabi 2021, his relationship with Max Verstappen, how it all came apart, and whether he wants back in. 58 minutes. New show for this list.

items.t: The Race F1 Rewind: The Truth Behind Schumacher's Ferrari Exit
items.d: Edd Straw and Mark Hughes dig into Michael Schumacher's 2006 departure from Ferrari after five titles and 72 wins, how the news broke, the theory that he was pushed out, and what might have happened if he had stayed. 49 minutes of pure F1 history. New show for this list.

items.t: Short Wave: The sound of fear, why so many animals scream
items.d: A Halloween-season dive into why marmot shrieks, baby cries, and horror soundtracks all hit the same nerve in us. A quick one for the drive in, 13 minutes.

items.t: The Indicator: CoreWeave woes, Pokemon foes, and maple syrup lows
items.d: The Indicator's weekly grab bag, out this morning: a Pokemon card heist, Canada's strategic maple syrup reserve running low, and one wobble in the AI credit market. 9 minutes.

items.t: Short Wave: The terrifying physics of prehistoric sea monsters
items.d: Mosasaurs were the bus-sized T. rex of the ocean, and a new study worked out how they hunted: far faster than any human swimmer, and sneaky. 9 minutes, and a good one to play for the kids.

more.t: F1 Beyond the Grid: Fred Vesti, making champions as Mercedes third driver
more.d: Tom Clarkson talks with Mercedes reserve Fred Vesti about the unseen job behind a title run: thousands of simulator laps, a say in which upgrades make the car, and staying ready to jump in for Russell or Antonelli, plus the party where he cornered Toto Wolff. 58 minutes.

more.t: The Indicator: Supercore inflation, Bumble valuation and Pooh's repatriation
more.d: Three quick indicators, including whether the original Winnie the Pooh dolls could leave the New York Public Library for England, and how Bumble went from doldrums to stock market darling. 9 minutes.

items.t: How to Design Flowers
items.d: A long interview with Nick Desnoyer, a plant biologist in Norwich who is building a petunia whose petals you can paint by dabbing small molecules on the buds to switch pigment genes on. Part mad-scientist garden tour, part serious genetics, ending with his dream of a flower design studio. Long: about 10,000 words, 40 minutes, so maybe one for the weekend.

items.t: What Is Gridification? The Hidden Shift in Recorded Music
items.d: Why does so much modern pop feel flat? This essay compares tempo data from 1975 and 2025 Billboard hits to show how performances are now snapped to a rigid grid in post-production, and argues that the tiny human push and pull of timing is what music is actually made of. About 1,600 words, 7 minutes.

items.t: The Phenomena That Brighten Dawn and Dusk
items.d: A short, clear nature column by a Colorado biologist on what you are looking at during sunrise and sunset: the blue band of Earth's own shadow climbing the sky, the pink Belt of Venus above it, and alpenglow on snowy peaks. Good ammunition for the next early morning with the kids. About 550 words, 3 minutes, from 2016 but timeless.

more.t: The Last Museum: Search 6 Million Artworks from the World's Museums
more.d: A free search engine across the public collections of the big museums, with semantic search so you can type something like 'red bicycle' and see what turns up. Browse time rather than reading time: 5 to 15 minutes of happy rabbit-holing.

more.t: Color Names: 31,970 Colors, Named by People
more.d: Paste any hex code or just scroll and find out that someone has named a shade 'Wine Dregs'. A pleasantly pointless, beautifully made catalog of crowd-named colors with a hand-picked best-of list. 5 minutes of browsing.

more.t: Railpass: Stare Out the Window of an Endless Train
more.d: A small web toy by designer Sami Smith: a rendered train carriage with real footage rolling past the window, for when you want to zone out on a long ride without buying a ticket. It takes about a minute to get the idea and as long as you like after that.

more.t: Dungeon Generation in the Gnomish Mines of NetHack
more.d: A short, code-free explanation of how the 1987 roguelike NetHack grows its organic cave levels: scatter random floor, run four rounds of a cellular automaton to clump and smooth it, then connect the leftover pockets with corridors. About 300 words, 2 minutes, plus a linked visualizer to play with.

items.t: The Art of the Thousand Bloom Chrysanthemum
items.d: One plant, eighteen months of pinching, tying and light control, and more than 1,000 flowers arranged in a perfect dome. A lovely piece on an odd Japanese horticultural tradition and the Longwood Gardens crew that keeps it alive in Pennsylvania. About 2,000 words, 11 minutes. New site for this list.

more.t: The Winners of the 2026 International Pano Awards
more.d: Kottke's picks from this year's best panoramic photography, plus the rule that makes a photo a pano (longest side at least twice the shortest). Five big wide images and about 100 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: 221 Camera Obscuras Fill Pneuhaus' Immersive, Inflatable, Image-Capturing Installation
more.d: A walk-in inflatable with 221 pinhole apertures that projects the sky and street onto soft bulging surfaces you can press to warp the picture, powered by nothing but sunlight. A bug's-eye view you would want to take the kids into. About 230 words plus photos, 2 minutes.

days.label: Thursday, October 22
days.note: New sites today: Wait But Why, Autosport, Crash.net, Smithsonian Magazine, Craig Mod, Aeon, Aftermath, Practical Engineering, and Construction Physics, plus two F1 podcasts new to the list, The Autosport F1 Podcast and Inside Line. Austin race week, and the Horner memoir keeps giving.

hero.alt: A group of friends gathered around a glowing campfire among tall trees at night in Haliburton, Canada
hero.caption: Fireside, Haliburton

items.t: Review: The 2027 Range Rover Electric Is the Most Radical Range Rover Yet
items.d: A real first drive, not a press release: Chris Chin takes a near-production prototype on road and through Land Rover's Gaydon off-road course and asks the only question that matters, does it still feel like a Range Rover. About 1,300 words, 7 minutes.

items.t: The James Brand Finally Built an EDC Multi-Tool to Rival the Swiss Army Knife
items.d: Hands-on time with the Helton, a $169 pocket multi-tool with four locking implements and nine functions, including the honest bit about finish already rubbing off the scales. About 900 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: Rivian's Rad Reinterpretation of an Iconic Movie Car Just Put Tesla on Notice
more.d: Rivian and Sony built a full-scale Ghostbusters Ecto-1 version of the R1S, with restored vintage roof sirens and a radar dish, and shipped a Halloween Mode update with themed lights, sounds and an in-car arcade game. Fun one to show the kids. About 500 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Work Sharp's Unique New EDC Knife Aims to Prove Less Really Is More
more.d: The RMX MisFit pairs a stubby 2.4 inch reverse tanto blade with a full-size magnesium handle and revives Work Sharp's switchable manual or automatic deployment, with a conversion kit in the box. About 600 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Swatch Group's German Sleeper Brand Drops a Fun Racing Chronograph
more.d: Union Glashutte's new 40mm Belisar Speedster takes its beige and orange checkerboard dial from a one-off 1968 Porsche 911, limited to 288 pieces at $3,700. About 450 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: An Affordable Automotive Icon Finally Rolls Into the 21st Century
more.d: Citroen's electric 2CV concept from the Paris show keeps the people's car brief: roughly one tonne, a single 8 inch screen, a target price near 15,000 euros and production confirmed for 2028. About 400 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: Leica Q3 43 Formula 1 Edition Camera
more.d: Quick look at Leica's F1 tie-in: a Q3 43 with a carbon fiber charging grip, red accents, steering-wheel-style grip covering and an app-only F1 color profile, at $9,950. Short blurb, about 120 words.

items.t: Japan's sample return mission to Phobos may also collect some Mars dust
items.d: Japan's MMX probe launched this week to land a rover on Mars's bigger moon, scoop up about 10 grams of it, and fly it home by 2031, with a bonus chance of catching grains blasted off Mars itself. A clear, timely explainer at about 950 words, roughly 4 minutes.

items.t: A Stunning Nebula Image Predicts How Our Sun Will Die
items.d: An astrophotographer's shot of the Dumbbell Nebula doubles as a preview of our own Sun's finale: red giant, shed outer layers, then a white dwarf lighting up the leftovers for 25,000 years. Quick and vivid, about 650 words or 3 minutes.

more.t: Horned dinosaurs' weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
more.d: Researchers stress-tested digital skulls of five horned dinosaurs and found Triceratops was built for horn-locking and wrestling, while earlier species were all show. About 800 words, a 3-minute read.

more.t: To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
more.d: From the Invisible Woman to ghost catfish and glasswing butterflies, a fun look at how real animals get close to transparent and why a true invisibility cloak remains out of reach. No math, about 600 words, 3 minutes.

more.t: Meet Loki the Sea Cucumber, One of 57 Newly Discovered Deep-Sea Species
more.d: A 21-day ROV expedition into a submarine canyon off Argentina turned up 57 new species, led by a translucent 4-inch sea cucumber named Loki. A quick, cheerful read of about 350 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: Ambient Earth
more.d: A 7.5-hour real-time 4K video of Earth from the Space Station, stitched from 49,000 astronaut photos with ambient audio recorded on board by Chris Hadfield. The post is a 1-minute read; the video is perfect for a second screen.

more.t: The Real Kevin Bacon
more.d: An interactive data essay that measures degrees of separation across 169,000 actors, finds Samuel L. Jackson is the true center of Hollywood, and simulates which young actor might take the crown next. About 900 words plus charts, 5 to 7 minutes.

items.t: The Fermi Paradox
items.d: Tim Urban's classic stick-figure tour of why a galaxy with maybe 100,000 intelligent civilizations looks completely empty, from the Great Filter to the galactic zoo theory. About 5,500 words, 24 minutes, and still the most fun explainer on the subject. New site for this list.

more.t: Twilight of the Velocipede: Typesetting Races before the Age of Linotype
more.d: In the 1870s and 1880s hand typesetters called Swifts raced in front of big crowds for $1,000 purses, and a Boston contest in 1886 featured record-breaking women compositors and two monkeys as distractions. About 3,000 words, 12 minutes, on a very clean site.

more.t: The Long History of the Quest to Find a Peak Taller Than Everest
more.d: Katie Ives traces a century of rumors, cloud-fooled surveyors and phantom Antarctic summits that convinced climbers something out there topped Everest. Book excerpt, about 1,800 words, 8 minutes.

items.t: Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians: What To Do Before 2026 Is Over
items.d: A checklist of moves to make before December 31 under the new tax rules: timing income and deductions, avoiding the AMT and underpayment penalties, topping off retirement and HSA accounts, charitable giving limits, the SALT cap, and when a Roth conversion makes sense. About 3,000 words, 13 minutes.

items.t: Why You (and I) Aren't Retiring
items.d: A columnist who hit financial independence at 45 and kept working digs into why so many high net worth doctors with modest spending still do not feel financially independent, from distrust of withdrawal-rate math to the pull of watching the number grow. About 1,300 words, 6 minutes.

more.t: What Is the Average Net Worth by Age?
more.d: Nick Maggiulli breaks down the Fed's new 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances by age and percentile, including the 45 to 54 bracket and what happens to the numbers once you strip out home equity. About 2,500 words, 11 minutes.

more.t: Market Risks
more.d: Adam Grossman on two risks that strong markets hide: how a 10 percent average return masks brutal single years, and why P/E ratios tell you almost nothing about the next 12 months. Ends with a Pascal's wager approach to allocation. About 1,000 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: Qualified Opportunity Zones Are Back
more.d: Jim Dahle explains the permanent new version of opportunity zone funds that starts January 2027: deferring capital gains, the 10 or 30 percent basis step-up, and why the real estate still has to be a good investment before the tax break matters. About 1,000 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: The Biggest Risk Everyone Already Knows About
more.d: Ben Carlson weighs the AI capex boom against past infrastructure bubbles, with the hyperscalers' debt funding, extreme index concentration, and Nvidia's surprisingly modest forward P/E on the other side of the ledger. Honest about not knowing how it ends. About 700 words, 4 minutes.
more.m: A Wealth of Common Sense, Oct 4

more.t: You're Not Rich, and Neither Am I
more.d: Dr. Flashy versus Dr. Net-Worth, two physicians with the same income and very different balance sheets, plus Fed and Medscape data on where doctors actually sit on the wealth curve. The point is spending deliberately, not just spending less. About 1,900 words, 9 minutes.

items.t: Five surprising things we learned from Horner's book
items.d: Edd Straw pulls the best gossip out of Christian Horner's new memoir: a Lotus test, a late-2012 approach from Niki Lauda to run Mercedes, and the Ricciardo handshake deal that fell apart. Roughly 700 words, a quick and fun read.

items.t: The maths behind when Mercedes could become F1 world champions in 2026
items.d: A clear walk through the title permutations heading into Austin: Antonelli's 102-point lead, why the drivers' crown is more likely to land in Mexico, and why Mercedes should wrap the constructors' title in Brazil. About 600 words. New site for this list.

items.t: F1 victory without a pitstop: Berger and Benetton's shock Mexican GP win
items.d: Matt Bishop marks 40 years since Gerhard Berger ran one set of Pirellis for all 68 laps in 1986 while Senna and Prost pitted, giving Benetton its first win and BMW's turbo its last. Good timing with Mexico up next week. About 1,700 words, an 8-minute read.

more.t: Early coronation for Antonelli? Five talking points for the United States Grand Prix
more.d: Keith Collantine's Austin preview: whether Antonelli can clinch this weekend (unlikely), whether a resurgent Verstappen and Red Bull keep winning, McLaren's post-Singapore tension, and the US teams' 2027 driver calls. About 500 words.

more.t: How Kimi Antonelli can become F1 world champion at the United States GP
more.d: The exact scenario for a title in Austin: Antonelli must win, Russell must finish ninth or lower, and Hamilton fifth or lower, with Russell's engine penalty possibly helping. About 700 words.

more.t: Lewis Hamilton magic or misery, Max Verstappen glory and more United States GP predictions
more.d: Five PlanetF1 writers make their calls for Austin, including a first Hamilton podium since 2022 and a Verstappen versus Antonelli fight for the win. About 800 words of fun pre-race opinion.

more.t: FIA president issues update on timeframe for mooted F1 V8 agreement
more.d: Mohammed Ben Sulayem wants V8s back in 2030, a year earlier than rumored, and needs four of six engine makers on board within months. About 550 words on where F1's engine future stands.

more.t: Antonelli reveals F1 championship hopes in meeting with NBA star
more.d: Antonelli dropped in on the San Antonio Spurs and met Victor Wembanyama, saying he hopes to have the title done within two weeks. Light and quick, about 380 words.

more.t: Mercedes target Austin fightback with upgrades after difficult Malaysia and Singapore races
more.d: Toto Wolff on why both Mercedes drivers get the new upgrade package this weekend and what went wrong in the last two rounds. About 350 words.

items.t: The Autosport F1 Podcast: Red Bull Sets the Pace, FIA Electronics Come Under Fire | Singapore Grand Prix 2026
items.d: Autosport veterans Stuart Codling and Kevin Turner ask whether Verstappen's Singapore sprint and race double means Red Bull now has the fastest car, with a clear explainer on tyre wear, why Leclerc and Hamilton faded, and what went wrong with the FIA's electronics in the rain. 40 minutes. New show for this list.

items.t: Inside Line F1 Podcast: Paddock Stories, Max Verstappen's Win, Lewis Hamilton's Error, FIA Delays, 2026 Singapore GP
items.d: Kunal Shah, who was in the Marina Bay paddock, brings behind-the-scenes stories from the weekend while Mithila Mehta and Soumil Arora debate Hamilton's puzzling strategy calls and why the race felt so flat. A quick, chatty listen at 31 minutes. Also new to this list.

items.t: 99% Invisible: Audio Guide of the Imperfections of a Perfect Masterpiece
items.d: A bonus walking tour of Frank Lloyd Wright's Guggenheim spiral that skips the greatness and lingers on the quirks: parapets repainted every night, the faint checkerboard left by sprayed concrete, and the 105 degree display bays that let art hang on a sloping ramp. 30 minutes.

items.t: Today, Explained: The passive income influencers
items.d: Sean Rameswaram digs into the online side hustle gurus who promise financial freedom for almost no work, and asks whether the whole passive income economy is just a pyramid scheme with better lighting. 27 minutes.

items.t: Twenty Thousand Hertz: Needle Drops, How pop songs first started showing up in movies
items.d: Dallas Taylor traces how pop songs got into movies, from a forgotten Broadway tune that became an unlikely hit to the rock and roll record that changed soundtracks forever, plus the happy accidents behind famous scenes of the 60s, 70s and 80s. Runs a bit long at 42 minutes but it is pure fun.

more.t: Grid Talk F1 Podcast: 2026 Singapore Review
more.d: Tom Downey and Jawad Yaqub, with guest Dev Tyagi, break down F1's first Singapore sprint weekend, Ferrari's strategy and McLaren's collisions, then run the title permutations for Austin, where Kimi Antonelli could clinch. 47 minutes.

more.t: Unexplainable: Talking with the dead
more.d: Cambridge researchers and psycholinguist Julie Sedivy consider AI deadbots that simulate lost loved ones, what those tools cost us, and the older, stranger ways people have always kept talking to the departed. Thoughtful rather than gloomy. 36 minutes.

more.t: 99% Invisible: Tony Hawk's Real-Life Willy Wonka
more.d: A profile of N.D. Austin, who builds sewer speakeasies, island coming-of-age rituals and a homemade desert train ride for Tony Hawk, and how a childhood in an Alaskan doomsday cult shaped his taste for everyday magic. 52 minutes.

items.t: Whatever Happened to Fire Escapes?
items.d: Grady Hillhouse traces how bolt-on iron fire escapes took over American cities after 1860s tenement fires, why engineers hated them almost from the start, and how New York finally banned new ones in 1968. A fun lesson in how building codes outlive their logic; about 2,700 words, or a 20 minute video if you would rather watch.

items.t: The Rise and Fall of the Plasma Screen
items.d: Brian Potter follows plasma displays from a 1960s University of Illinois teaching computer through bank terminals and military gear to the living room, and explains exactly why LCD beat it on heat, brightness, and factory yield. Clean, chart-light engineering history, about 2,100 words.

items.t: In Hilbert Space, All Things Are Quantumly Possible
items.d: Charlie Wood gives the friendliest explanation you will find of the mathematical space where quantum states live, how von Neumann stitched two rival theories into one in 1927, and why physicists still argue over whether it is real. About 1,500 words, no equations required.

more.t: Good Type Against All Odds
more.d: Marcin Wichary collects tiny, unexpectedly lovely typographic details from pixel displays, engraved keyboard caps, and old typesetting machines, and asks why anyone bothered to get them right. Short and picture-heavy, about 300 words plus a dozen close-up photos, five minutes.

more.t: Plasticorals: A New Kind of Plastic Pollution Fused Into Coral Rubble
more.d: Researchers in Okinawa found melted household plastic welded into dead coral on local beaches, probably from beach bonfires, and gave the stuff a name. A quick, slightly eerie piece of natural history with good photos, about 500 words.

more.t: The Best Way to Play Super Mario 64: On Apple Vision Pro
more.d: Michael Steil turns every Mario 64 level into a tabletop diorama you walk around in a headset while playing with a normal controller, built on the fan decompilation projects. Mostly video clips with a short writeup, about 300 words and a few minutes of footage.

more.t: Sixteen Years After Deepwater Horizon, Deep Sea Life Shows Few Signs of Recovery
more.d: A new PNAS study finds deep-sea squid, octopus, krill, and lanternfish populations in the Gulf dropped at least 60 percent after the 2010 spill and have not bounced back. A sobering but quick read, about 300 words.

items.t: The Roman coffin hiding in Westminster Abbey
items.d: A stone sarcophagus dug up at Westminster Abbey in 1869 turns out to be a Roman coffin that was carved with a cross and recycled around the year 1000 to bury a medieval abbot, then looted twice. A tidy detective story with radiocarbon dates and a named original owner, about 1,100 words. New site for this list.

more.t: Walking Norway's Gudbrandsdalsleden pilgrimage
more.d: Craig Mod walks 132 km of the old St. Olav's Way to Trondheim with Kevin Kelly and friends: barley fields, farm stays, a comically small bed, and evening debates about what makes a great day. Uncrowded trail inspiration in about 1,300 words with photos.

more.t: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies
more.d: Melanie Challenger argues that GPS, phones and AI quietly erode skills your body evolved to own, from wayfinding to memory, and that the body-as-machine metaphor was never a good one. A thoughtful 3,400-word essay, about 17 minutes, with a free audio version.

more.t: Triple-A Minesweeper
more.d: A short, funny post about Mike Lacher's browser game that reboots Windows Minesweeper as a bloated blockbuster, complete with yellow-paint hints, an opening credits roll and a hero who keeps announcing he needs to sweep these mines. Two minutes to read, with a link to play it free in your browser.

days.label: Wednesday, October 21
days.note: New sites today: Longreads, Early Retirement Now, Mr. Money Mustache, GPblog, RacingNews365, Open Culture, Short Wave, and a Nebraska newsroom with a hot dog cannon. Each slot now folds a few extras under a toggle.

hero.alt: A surfer riding a small wave on golden sunlit water at sunset
hero.caption: Golden hour surf

items.t: The lost art of carrying loads
items.d: A tour of how people around the world have hauled heavy things for centuries, from Japanese furoshiki cloths and Himalayan tumpline baskets to birch-bark packs and head carrying, and what modern backpack designers could learn from them. About 3,000 words, 15 to 20 minutes.

items.t: Storyteller's clever new modular camper van makes gear a priority, too
items.d: Storyteller's new Gear Mode Sprinter conversion has wall panels that flip between cargo bay, bunks, and dinette, so bikes and boards ride inside with the family. About 500 words, a quick daydream read.

more.t: Wait, did Fossil just make a great automatic watch?
more.d: The mall-watch brand of your high school years is back with Swiss automatic movements and a mid-priced Signature CS-1 line, and Gear Patrol is cautiously impressed. About 850 words.

more.t: Outerknown outshines Patagonia at its own game with a premium fleece lineup
more.d: Why recycled wool might beat polyester fleece for breathability, warmth when wet, and stink resistance, hung on Outerknown's new Woolaroo line. About 500 words.

more.t: Yeti's new under-the-radar release is practical, backwards compatible and budget-friendly
more.d: Yeti quietly fixed the fiddly four-piece lid on its Travel Mug with a leakproof three-piece Stronghold Lid that fits older mugs too. About 700 words.

items.t: Whoa, the Lion Nebula!
items.d: A fresh James Webb infrared portrait of the Lion Nebula, the glowing bubble a dying Sun-like star leaves behind, with a plain-language explainer on the lion's face, mane, and comet-like tufts of dust. A two-minute look at a gorgeous image that will be gone in about 10,000 years.

items.t: Voyager 1 is now one light-day from Earth. What's out there?
items.d: On November 18 the 1977 probe becomes the first human-made object a full light-day away, and this piece walks through what it has found at the edge of the solar system and the unexplained readings it has sent back since 2020. About 1,700 words, 9 minutes.

more.t: This giant waterlily species was discovered via Instagram
more.d: A botanist's Instagram selfie tipped off Kew's waterlily expert to a plant growing far outside its known range in Colombia, and a scramble up the Inirida River turned up a new six-foot-wide species with only 30 to 50 plants left. About 400 words.

more.t: Astronomers find first green star
more.d: Stars are never supposed to look green, but a cool white dwarf that swallowed its own planets now glows chartreuse because sodium in its atmosphere soaks up the orange light. About 600 words, with a salmon-pink star as a bonus.

more.t: How hunting owls use sound to see under the snow
more.d: A short clip from CBC's The Nature of Things uses a 60-microphone acoustic camera to show what a great grey owl hears through half a meter of snow before it dives on a vole. Quick post plus a short video, good for the kids too.

more.t: How the Grand Canyon could have lost 1 billion years of geologic history
more.d: A new idea for the famous gap in the canyon's rock record: a continent-spanning cliff that formed as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart and eroded a billion years of rock away. 3-minute read.

items.t: Still on its way to Cleveland
items.d: In fall 1996 a Michigan couple loaded three kids and a golden retriever into a motorhome and spent nine months and 25,000 miles crossing 40 states, filing a family travel website over dial-up from libraries and strangers' offices along the way. A warm, funny memoir of a big family adventure and the friendlier early internet that made it possible, about 2,700 words (10 to 14 minutes). New site for this list.

more.t: Death by a thousand dams
more.d: Ben Goldfarb on the tens of thousands of small, forgotten mill dams across the Northeast that still block alewives and shad, and the people pulling them out one creek at a time to bring the fish runs back. Free and ad-free on nonprofit bioGraphic, about 4,400 words (roughly 20 minutes). New site for this list.

more.t: Where the forest went
more.d: In 1788 a surveyor named Hugh Maxwell walked straight lines through 2.6 million acres of western New York forest and turned it into a grid of parcels for sale; the author retraces his route through what is now suburbia. About 5,900 words (25 minutes).

items.t: Can a TIPS allocation raise my safe withdrawal rate?
items.d: Big ERN reverses his old skepticism on TIPS now that 20- and 30-year real yields sit above 3 percent, and runs the simulations showing a partial TIPS ladder can lift a safe withdrawal rate toward 5 percent in a tax-advantaged account. Dense but rigorous, about 25 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: Will the AI bubble destroy our retirement?
items.d: MMM zooms out to show how 2008 and 2020 look like blips on a 20-year chart, then argues the real portfolio risk is your own fear reflex, with practical rules for managing it. Upbeat, about 2,000 words. New site for this list.

more.t: Some thoughts on spending
more.d: JL Collins on how to spend without guilt once you have enough, including why a poor-value splurge like a first-class seat can still be the right call. An 11-minute evergreen read. New site for this list.

more.t: Long-term money
more.d: Morgan Housel on why each generation works so the next can have it easier, and why the kids who benefit look spoiled rather than lucky. A quick 800-word read for anyone saving for young children. New site for this list.

more.t: The shockingly simple math behind Social Security
more.d: Treats your future Social Security as a present-value asset you already own and shows how much it shrinks the savings target for someone in their 40s. About 2,200 words with a worked example on claiming at 62 versus later.

items.t: Analysis: Max Verstappen up to three seconds slower in Austin
items.d: Austin preview with a twist: GPblog runs the numbers on how much slower the 2026 cars will be around COTA than Verstappen's 2025 pole lap (about 2.8 seconds) and where the time goes, in the fast esses and on the straight where battery energy runs out. About 1,000 words, 5 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: Exclusive: Red Bull reveal knife-edge battle as Max Verstappen confidence builds
items.d: Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache explains why the RB22 was so hard to balance between low-speed traction and high-speed stability, and how the Baku floor and diffuser package turned the car into a two-race winner. A rare peek inside the engineering before Austin, about 3 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: MPH: The revelation in Horner's book, how he turned Red Bull from no-hopers into F1 winners
items.d: Mark Hughes reads Christian Horner's new memoir Drive and pulls out the story of how a struggling ex-Jaguar outfit landed Adrian Newey in 2006 and the friction that followed. Good team-building history with some fresh gossip, about 950 words, 5 minutes.

more.t: Youngest world champion in F1 history? The records Kimi Antonelli is closing in on
more.d: What has to happen in Austin for Antonelli to clinch the title at 20, plus the Vettel, Hamilton and Mercedes records he is chasing. About 950 words, 5 minutes. New site for this list.

more.t: Featured comment: Budget cap not to blame for lack of winning teams in F1
more.d: Keith Collantine spotlights a reader who counted only six wins from outside the top four teams in roughly 600 races between 1990 and 2023, an argument that money, not the cost cap, keeps the winners' circle small. About 400 words, 2 minutes.

more.t: Horner was congratulated by Red Bull bosses after F1 engine's wins
more.d: Horner says the shareholders who fired him thanked him when the in-house Red Bull engine he championed won its first races this year. Gossip with a sting, about 775 words, 4 minutes.

more.t: On This Day: Hill claims emotional championship victory for Williams at Suzuka
more.d: Thirty years ago this month Damon Hill won the title in his last race for Williams, the team that had already shown him the door. A one-minute history nugget from Keith Collantine.

more.t: Lewis Hamilton delivers blunt assessment on common F1 track feature
more.d: Hamilton says he misses grass and gravel run-offs and names his toughest physical seasons, a quick read before a weekend at tarmac-heavy COTA. About 350 words, 2 minutes.

items.t: Motor Sport F1 Show: Ferrari F1 comms blunders, 'Hamilton asked a really easy question!'
items.d: Mark Hughes and Bryn Lucas trace Ferrari's radio and strategy communication problems back to the Vettel era and explain why drivers stop trusting the pit wall, then take listener questions on those odd rear-wing triangles and on F1's planned Rwanda race. 57 minutes.

items.t: P1 with Matt and Tommy: Our 2026 United States GP predictions
items.d: A light race-week preview for Austin with pole and winner picks, driver-market chatter about Haas and Raphael Kamara, and how teams use private testing to find lap time. 34 minutes.

items.t: Unexplainable: What color is a tennis ball?
items.d: Yellow or green? Neuroscientist and artist Bevil Conway argues there may be no such thing as color at all, which makes this a fun one to settle with the kids. 28 minutes.

items.t: Planet Money: Charles Ponzi's scheme (plus a new scam)
items.d: How an Italian immigrant with a postal reply coupon and no money became a household name for fraud, based on Mitchell Zuckoff's book, with a modern scam tacked on at the end. 26 minutes.

items.t: Short Wave: What are the odds we're not alone in the universe?
items.d: A quick walk through the Drake Equation and whether the 1961 formula still guides the search for alien life. 15 minutes, so a short one for the last stretch of the drive. New show for this list.

more.t: Missed Apex: Behind the Barriers, Campbell Waddell
more.d: An interview with Dr Campbell Waddell, whose PhD on motorsport surfaces turned into 20 years working on F1 circuits around the world, covering how asphalt and tires interact plus the story of an F1 driver accidentally hitting him in the face with a door. A long one at 64 minutes. New show for this list.

more.t: Unexplainable: How does music move us? (feat. Sylvan Esso's Amelia Meath)
more.d: Why a song can give you goosebumps or make you cry, with singer Amelia Meath and Princeton music cognition researcher Elizabeth Margulis. 32 minutes.

more.t: Planet Money: Where all those weird new drinks are coming from
more.d: A visit to the beverage lab behind the flood of functional sodas and strange seltzers, including a taste test of a sports hydration broth. 30 minutes.

items.t: Der Viener Schlinger: the meat cannon that launched 20,000 hot dogs
items.d: A Nebraska nonprofit newsroom tells the full story of the handheld hot dog launcher that has fired wieners into the Memorial Stadium crowd at Husker games since 1997, from its radio-contest name to the student engineers who kept improving it. Long and very fun, about 4,000 words (19 minutes). New site for this list.

items.t: Flat pack, step by step: IKEA manuals built in 3D
items.d: Ryan Sael pairs the real IKEA instruction pages for the BILLY bookcase and the LACK table with an interactive 3D build you can step through, play end to end, or explode apart, plus a short explainer on how cam locks actually work. Ten minutes of poking around, oddly satisfying.

items.t: William Gibson and the trademarking of Cyberspace
items.d: Eric Gullichsen, who was at Autodesk when the company tried to trademark the word cyberspace around 1989, sets the record straight on Gibson's objection and the long-running myth (a Timothy Leary prank) that Gibson trademarked Gullichsen's name in revenge. Short, about 600 words.

more.t: Permit Pending: SimCity, but with permits
more.d: A free browser city builder (no account, desktop only) where you are an elected mayor rather than a god, so every new road, apartment block or factory has to survive zoning boards, angry neighbors, lawsuits and the next election. Satirical premise, real game.

more.t: Weball: play Katamari on any website
more.d: Type in any URL and roll a Katamari-style ball around the page, scooping up words, images and buttons as it grows. Silly five-minute toy, no sign-in.

more.t: Making solar panels with a microwave (video)
more.d: The Dr.Semiconductor channel fabricates working silicon solar cells in a home garage using a 900 watt microwave, a microwave kiln and bare wafers, as a demonstration of what hobby gear can do versus a real chip fab.

items.t: In 1897, London's lampposts dispensed hot coffee, tea, and fluid beef
items.d: The Pluto Lamp was a Victorian streetlight that sold a ha'penny cup of hot coffee, tea, cocoa, or beef broth, plus postcards and cigarettes, until counterfeit coins and upkeep killed it before 1900. About 430 words, a two-minute curiosity. New site for this list.

more.t: The best Monopoly strategy, tested on 300 million games
more.d: A simulation of 313 million Monopoly games finds the best strategy wins 43 percent of four-player games and the worst just 3 percent, and names the four mistakes that make the difference. Short post pointing to a YouTube breakdown, handy before the next family game night.

more.t: In 'Aeolus,' DRIFT suspends illuminated glass rods in a sculpture of the wind
more.d: Amsterdam studio DRIFT hung hundreds of lit glass rods that ripple when visitors move past, so the sculpture only exists when someone is in the room. One-minute read with photos. New site for this list.

more.t: Interactive map of the Hebrew Bible
more.d: Nathan Yau points to Torahmap, which lays out every verse of the Hebrew Bible as a zoomable grid, one column per book, one square per verse, a neat example of treating words as data. One-minute post that links out to the project. New site for this list.

days.label: Tuesday, October 20
days.note: Fresh sites all over today: Carryology, Science News, Big Think, Atlas Obscura, Humble Dollar, A Wealth of Common Sense, Motor Sport Magazine, Motorsport Week, and a map blog.

hero.alt: A man fly fishing on the Owens River at sunset with snow-capped mountains behind him
hero.caption: Owens River, dusk

items.t: The forgotten British brand that changed outdoor gear forever
items.d: The rise and fall of Karrimor, the Lancashire bike-bag shop that invented the Karrimat sleeping pad and built the packs carried up Everest in 1975, then got crushed by cheap imports. Gear history rather than a product plug. New site for this list.

items.t: This legendary mil-spec dive watch now has a permanent titanium upgrade
items.d: Marathon's GSAR, the dive watch actually issued to search-and-rescue units, finally gets a regular-production titanium case about 30 percent lighter, with tritium tubes and a 24-hour military dial. A quick look at a tool watch built for use rather than show.

items.t: These tiny snakes cartwheel to escape danger
items.d: Researchers put little Southeast Asian snakes on a lab racetrack and filmed them flinging themselves into airborne cartwheels at up to 13 km/h, which finally explains the old hoop snake legend. About 700 words, with video. New site for this list.

items.t: 7 shocking comparisons between the Universe and a human body
items.d: Ethan Siegel lines up the numbers in you (cells, atoms, daily cell turnover) against the numbers out there (stars, galaxies, cosmic structures) and the matchups are surprising. No math, roughly 8 minutes.

items.t: The history and mystery of Yemen's 'Well of Hell'
items.d: For centuries locals avoided a 367-foot sinkhole in the Yemeni desert said to be a prison for jinn, until a geologist's team rappelled to the bottom and found waterfalls, cave pearls, and a surprisingly friendly ecosystem. About 1,350 words, 6 or 7 minutes.

items.t: Life insurance
items.d: Adam Grossman uses Pacific Life's $58 million settlement over permanent life insurance marketing to make the case for plain term coverage, then walks through how to size it: mortgage balance, future tuition, a living-expense fund, and separate policies for each working spouse. A tight refresher for a high earner with young kids, about 5 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: Is it time to rebalance your portfolio?
items.d: Ben Carlson shows how the 2020s bull market has quietly pushed a 60/40 portfolio to roughly 77/23, and argues that with high-quality bond yields above 5 percent a balanced allocation no longer needs heroic stock returns. Short and practical, about 3 minutes.
items.m: A Wealth of Common Sense, Oct 13

items.t: Why has Valtteri Bottas lost his F1 race pace? The 'million-dollar question'
items.d: Pablo Elizalde digs into why Bottas qualifies close to Cadillac teammate Sergio Perez but loses the race head-to-head 11 to 4, weighing set-up, car inconsistency, and Bottas himself without rushing to a verdict. About 5 minutes.

items.t: It's race week: 5 storylines ahead of the 2026 United States Grand Prix
items.d: Chris Medland sets up Austin, where Antonelli can clinch the title with a win if Russell and Hamilton stumble, and explains why Verstappen's winning run (he is 119 points back) has Mercedes calling his form 'very, very scary'. Also the upgrade race and Haas signing Rafael Camara. About 5 minutes.

items.t: F1 Rewind: Jenson Button completes Brawn's one pound miracle in Sao Paulo
items.d: Timely history as another title could be decided this weekend: how Ross Brawn bought the Honda team for a pound, dominated early 2009, then watched Button fight from a Q2 exit to the fifth place that sealed the championship at Interlagos. About 3 minutes. New site for this list.

items.t: The Race F1 Podcast: Christian Horner on Ferrari rumors, nearly signing Alonso, and Newey's Aston Martin
items.d: A 56 minute long-form interview with the former Red Bull boss, out days before his book lands. Edd Straw and Jon Noble get him on building Red Bull from disruptor to dynasty, why he was pushed out, his conditions for a comeback, and how the Ferrari rumors started.

items.t: Bring Back V10s: Debating your 'V10sMen' suggestions
items.d: A 36 minute bonus episode where Glenn Freeman and Matt argue over which listener-nominated V10 era cult heroes (Salo, Fisichella, Panis, Herbert) actually earn the badge. Pure 1990s and 2000s nostalgia with no race recap in sight.

items.t: Science Vs: Collagen peptides, should you take them?
items.d: Wendy Zukerman spends 35 minutes testing the influencer claims that collagen powders make you look younger and recover faster, with dermatologists and exercise physiologists explaining what actually happens to collagen once you swallow it.

items.t: Planet Money: Wanna slow down AI? These biologists can help
items.d: A 29 minute history lesson about the 1975 Asilomar meeting, when scientists voluntarily paused gene-splicing research for four days on the California coast, and whether that playbook could work again. A fun collective action puzzle told as a story.

items.t: I built a drone with only one motor
items.d: Maker Joshua Bird builds a flying drone that steers with a single motor, working through failed hub designs, timing fixes, a homemade high-speed camera, and a test stand before it finally flies. Satisfying garage engineering, with open-source CAD files if you want to poke at the design.

items.t: Gdynia and the dream of a maritime Poland
items.d: In 1920 a newly independent Poland, boxed in by Germany and the German-run Free City of Danzig, picked a fishing village and built a modernist port city from scratch in under two decades. A compact history of ambition, architecture, and the limits of a harbor in guaranteeing a country's security.

items.t: Dogs seem to agree with humans that 'bouba' is round and 'kiki' is spiky
items.d: Researchers at the University of Parma tested 70 dogs and found they looked longer at the round shape for 'bouba' and the spiky one for 'kiki', the same sound-shape instinct people have. A three minute oddity.

items.t: There are 89,603 dogs in New York City
items.d: A short post on Every Dog in New York, an interactive map built from the city's dog licensing records that shows the dominant breed and most popular names in each of 197 neighborhoods, plus the 2020 puppy spike and the end of the French Bulldog boom. Fun to poke around in for ten minutes. New site for this list.

days.label: Monday, October 19
days.note: Automated edition, with two F1 podcasts and a third F1 site added mid-morning.

items.t: Ornot's waterproof, packable new cycling jacket thought of everything
items.d: A real hands-on test, ridden in the rain from Manhattan to Queens. The stuff-sack pocket and two-way zipper are the details that win it over.

items.t: Leisure Travel Vans Wonder FX motorhome
items.d: A sub-25-foot Transit-based camper with a Murphy bed and optional AWD. One-minute daydream material.

items.t: Triplet of 'ghostly' galaxies hints at what dark matter is, and isn't
items.d: Three faint galaxies seem to have almost no dark matter, and the best explanation is an ancient collision that stripped it away. A cosmic whodunit, about 7 minutes.

items.t: Here's how freaky the universe would look if light slowed to 3 miles per hour
items.d: A short piece about a browser toy that lets you walk around a world where light moves at walking pace. Three minutes to read, then something to click on.

items.t: Portrait of a Scaphander
items.d: From the Belgica's brutal Antarctic winter of 1898 to the first underwater photographs and blind cave creatures, following the naturalist Emil Racovita. About 3,800 words.

items.t: 11 retirement planning mistakes that haunt high-earning physicians
items.d: Mid-career traps: too much pre-tax money that becomes an RMD and IRMAA problem, SEP IRA instead of a Solo 401(k) or cash balance plan, and deadlines that fall well before December.

items.t: Who got richer since 2022?
items.d: New Fed data: households over 75 gained about 38 percent while the under-35s lost ground. Maggiulli's takeaway is to give to your kids earlier. 9 minutes.

items.t: What one image can't show you about the Rwanda F1 track
items.d: Alex Wurz walks through the elevation and braking zones of the new Kigali circuit that a single render cannot convey. 6 minutes.

items.t: Toto Wolff issues reality check as Kimi Antonelli closes in on the title
items.d: Antonelli is 102 points clear and can clinch in Austin with a win and the right gap to Russell and Hamilton. Wolff doubts it happens this weekend.

items.t: Singapore victory leaves Verstappen one win away from a full set, but not for long
items.d: Keith Collantine's stats column: 73rd win from pole leading every lap, a 27th different winning circuit, and only Madrid left to complete the set. New site for this list.

items.t: F1 Beyond the Grid: 50 years since James Hunt's dramatic title win, with Freddie Hunt
items.d: 25 minutes. Tom Clarkson and Hunt's son on the 1976 season, the Nurburgring fire, the Fuji decider, and growing up with a maverick champion for a father.

items.t: F1 Nation: F1 Explains, the grid and what happens before lights out
items.d: 41 minutes. What the mechanics and drivers actually do in the half hour before a start, with Zhou Guanyu as the guest.

items.t: Planet Money: Anatomy of a movie market
items.d: 32 minutes. Riding along with the 'King of Sundance' as he sells a slate of indie films to Netflix, Sony and Apple, with the backstories of Little Miss Sunshine and Napoleon Dynamite.

items.t: Unexplainable: What's cooler than being cool?
items.d: 29 minutes. Why quantum computers have to be chilled to near the coldest temperatures in the universe, and the race to build the refrigerators that get them there.

items.t: Today, Explained: The cost of loving your pet
items.d: 30 minutes. How our bonds with pets deepened after the pandemic, and how the bills climbed with them.

items.t: I electrified my push scooter with a power drill
items.d: A cordless drill bolted to the front wheel of a Razor scooter, with one-way bearings so it still coasts. About 10 mph and 2 miles of range. Did not save money, was worth it anyway.

items.t: World first: a southern ground hornbill gets 3D printed beak prostheses at Artis Zoo
items.d: Amsterdam's zoo and Utrecht's vets rebuilt a broken beak in two printed pieces. The bird started using it the same day.

items.t: There's never been a better time to go into math
items.d: Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown on why AI proving theorems makes math more inviting, not less. A 35 minute video, so save it for a lunch break.

items.t: Why some people mow a lawn better than others
items.d: Mow a virtual lawn as efficiently as you can, then see how your route compares with 132,000 other people and the mathematically optimal path. Oddly competitive.

hero.alt: A lone two lane highway runs straight across the Atacama Desert toward distant mountains
hero.caption: Lone desert highway

items.t: Yeti's first technical jacket should put Patagonia and The North Face on notice
items.d: The cooler company made a shell. Gear Patrol thinks it is a real contender.

items.t: Ressence Type 10 DN
items.d: A watch with no hands: oil-filled discs rotate inside each other. 100 made.

items.t: Sea monkeys show scientists how to rewrite a rule of turbulence
items.d: Brine shrimp swimming in a tank reversed the direction energy is supposed to flow in turbulent water.

items.t: Life after death?
items.d: Thousands of people answered what they think comes next. A scrolling visual essay, about 8 minutes.

items.t: Jos Verstappen was hyped like Max, until it all went wrong
items.d: The father's career, which explains a lot about the son.

items.t: Invest vs. pay off debt: what should you do with extra cash?
items.d: Listener questions on debt payoff versus investing, practice buy-ins, and account types.

items.t: 'My spirit animal is now the sloth': how real retirees withdraw money
items.d: Survey answers from retired physicians on how they actually spend down.

items.t: How Horner, Brown and Wolff made their fortunes from F1
items.d: UK company accounts, so the numbers are real. Horner's exit payment is the headline.

items.t: What Ferrari is changing with its biggest upgrade of 2026
items.d: New floor for Austin this weekend, the last big push before the 2027 car.

items.t: Chequered Flag Extra: F1 super subs and the home Grand Prix curse
items.d: Latest episode, 30 minutes. Streams free on BBC Sounds without an account.

items.t: 99% Invisible: (Not Just) Another Brick in the Wall
items.d: 28 minutes on Chicago's strange handmade bricks and why they look the way they do.

items.t: Today, Explained: Data centers fight back
items.d: 26 minutes. The PR war to make AI infrastructure likable.

items.t: Sigsaly: Churchill's top secret hotline to the President
items.d: The encrypted phone in the Cabinet War Rooms, and how it worked.

items.t: The Zelda timeline, to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake
items.d: A fan-built interactive timeline of every game. Pure nostalgia.

items.t: Going 94 mph on a skateboard, new world record
items.d: Diego Poncelet, 151.8 km/h, downhill. Watch the video before coffee.

items.t: The online Library of Babel
items.d: Every possible page of text already exists here. Search for a sentence you just wrote and it will find it.

hero.alt: A runner on a ridge above the clouds
hero.caption: Ridge running
